transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-29
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam, Maya, Elliot (Sunrise)

Summary:
Quick discovery to determine fit for Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) for Sunrise Merchant's checkout recommendation service. Goal: understand traffic profile, latency targets, security constraints, and plan time-to-first-token (quickstart) and a short pilot.

Topics:
- Current architecture / stack
- Latency & cost targets for inference
- Data residency and encryption needs (KMS, audit logs)
- Quickstart/free credits and time-to-first-token path
- Pilot success criteria and timeline

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, quick intros — I'll let Priya do a quick tech intro too, but high level we're here to figure out the best way Sunrise can get to production quickly with Redwood, whether that's the hosted API to start or going straight to a dedicated or private deploy.

[00:00:22] Maya Flores: Yeah thanks Jordan. I'm Maya, CTO at Sunrise, we run the merchant checkout and recommendation engine. With peaks on holiday we see spikes up to, like, 1.2k rps for some endpoints. We want to introduce LLM-based suggestions at the checkout but worried about latency and PII.

[00:00:38] Liam O'Connor: Liam here — head of platform — main things for us: sub-150ms 95th percentile is sort of our ideal for these user-facing calls, and we also need SOC 2 type controls, SSO, and KMS integration.

[00:00:55] Priya Desai: Great — hi all, SE at Redwood. Okay, couple quick clarifying q's: 1) Are you thinking to replace your existing recommendation service or run LLM as an assist layer? 2) Typical prompt size and expected response length?

[00:01:08] Elliot Wu: We're looking at an assist layer initially—keep the current rule-based fallback. Prompt sizes vary but usually ~200 tokens in, 150 tokens out on average, sometimes up to 512 tokens for longer explanations. Peak concurrency for the feature will be around 200 concurrent requests during spikes.

[00:01:30] Jordan Kim: Perfect, that's super actionable. So quick mapping — hosted API (Redwood API) is fastest to get started: self-serve, redeem credits, get tokens flowing. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower unit cost at scale, and private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict isolation and customer-managed networking. We can help you map based on your latency and compliance needs.

[00:01:52] Maya Flores: For hosted, how do you handle data retention? We can't keep PII in logs in plaintext.

[00:02:05] Priya Desai: We have configurable retention and redaction settings; hosted still supports encryption in transit and at rest, and we can integrate with your KMS for key management. That said, for some regulated data customers choose private or dedicated plus VPC peering to reduce blast radius.

[00:02:23] Liam O'Connor: KMS integration would be a must for us, plus audit logs for every model call. Is that available on the self-serve hosted tier or only enterprise?

[00:02:36] Jordan Kim: KMS tying and audit logs are available on Redwood Dedicated and Private by default; for hosted we have audit logs as an add-on for enterprise plans. We'll include a matrix in the doc I'll send.

[00:02:52] Maya Flores: Latency — you said hosted first. Can hosted meet our sub-150ms target for 512 token exchanges?

[00:03:05] Priya Desai: Real talk: sub-150ms 95p for 512 tokens is challenging on many models, even on dedicated hardware — unless you're using extremely optimized quantized variants and a dedicated pool with continuous batching tuned to your workload. For hosted, typical 95p for 512 tokens might be 200–350ms depending on model and region. For short prompts (200 in / 150 out) it's more achievable. We can run an eval using your payloads.

[00:03:31] Elliot Wu: Hmm, ok. So maybe we start hosted for quick experiments and then move to dedicated for the production rollout. How quick is time-to-first-token — like, what's realistic for our engineers to get a call out?

[00:03:45] Jordan Kim: Time-to-first-token (TTFT) for self-serve customers is usually under a day: sign up, redeem credits, API key, and hit the endpoint with our SDK. For a full integration with SSO and KMS we should expect a couple weeks. For pilot purposes you can be calling in hours once you have the sample prompts.

[00:04:03] Maya Flores: Credits — what do you offer for POCs?

[00:04:09] Jordan Kim: We can provide an initial credit allocation — typically 30k tokens for PLG/quickstart trials. I'll send the redemption link. If you want Dedicated pilot credits we can discuss a short reserved capacity window.

[00:04:21] Liam O'Connor: On the security front, is there a SOC 2 report we can review? And SAML SSO?

[00:04:29] Priya Desai: Yes, SOC 2 Type II report is available under NDA; SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning is supported. We'll add both links to the packet.

[00:04:40] Maya Flores: Good. What about model selection and quality — we need guardrails against hallucination for checkout text that could suggest wrong discounts or wrong legal language.

[00:04:52] Priya Desai: We recommend a curated model from our catalog and a baseline set of prompt-level safety checks. Redwood Optimize can help with quantization and cost/perf tuning, and we can set up evals tied to your prompt sets so we can alert on regressions. Also suggest a canary rollout — you can route a small percentage to new model variants.

[00:05:14] Liam O'Connor: Concurrency: we said 200 concurrent during peaks — what's your advice for batching and cost?

[00:05:23] Priya Desai: We use continuous batching; batching helps reduce unit cost but can increase tail latency. For user-facing sub-150ms SLOs, we usually keep batch windows tight and use prefix caching where repetitive patterns exist. For your peak concurrency, a dedicated pool sized to handle base concurrency with headroom for spikes is ideal. We'll give a sizing suggestion once you share traffic patterns.

[00:05:44] Elliot Wu: On the private option, is the control plane still managed by Redwood? We need to know if we can run the control plane on our VPC or if it's fully air-gapped on-prem.

[00:05:54] Jordan Kim: Both options exist — private deployment can be a customer-managed control plane in your VPC, or an on-prem package for highly regulated setups. Management ops differ of course; on-prem requires more time for install and security reviews.

[00:06:07] Maya Flores: Pricing — ballpark numbers for dedicated? We want to evaluate tradeoffs against OpenAI and a potential self-hosted GPU partner.

[00:06:17] Priya Desai: Ballpark: dedicated pricing depends on GPU type and reserved capacity; rough guidance: once you're at production QPS and consistent throughput, dedicated reduces per-token unit cost substantially vs hosted. We'll provide a cost comparison sheet that includes approximate TCO vs OpenAI and a self-hosted infra estimate.

[00:06:35] Liam O'Connor: Great. For pilot success criteria, what do you recommend?

[00:06:41] Jordan Kim: Recommend 4 success metrics: 1) performance — meet 95p latency threshold for target prompt size; 2) cost — unit cost within acceptable range vs business KPIs; 3) quality — pass X% of safety/accuracy checks; 4) ops — integration with SSO/KMS and ingestion of audit logs. If those are green within the pilot window we can expand.

[00:07:01] Maya Flores: Timeline — how long is the pilot? We can commit engineering time for two weeks if we go hosted; longer for private.

[00:07:09] Jordan Kim: Typical pilot: 2–4 weeks for hosted -> dedicated pilot; private pilots often take 4–8 weeks depending on networking approvals. We can frontload quick wins with hosted (TTFT in hours) and then schedule a dedicated sizing/benchmarks phase.

[00:07:24] Elliot Wu: One practical question — are SDKs available for our stack? We use Node services fronting an express layer and Rust for some internal microservices.

[00:07:33] Priya Desai: Yes, official SDKs for Node and Python, plus a generic HTTP REST interface you can call from Rust. We also have streaming and functions/tool-calling features if you want structured outputs.

[00:07:47] Liam O'Connor: Any gotchas we should expect when importing model outputs into downstream systems? For instance, tokenization differences or deterministic output concerns?

[00:07:58] Priya Desai: Tokenization differences can affect cost estimates; we'll include tokenization examples. For determinism, we recommend seeding and temperature controls for critical sections. For transactional text (legal or monetary), we advise strict validation layers — don't auto-apply anything without a verification step.

[00:08:16] Jordan Kim: Okay, quick recap and concrete next steps — we'll send a short packet: quickstart guide + 30k credit redemption link, security and SOC2 docs under NDA, a matrix comparing hosted/dedicated/private features (KMS, audit logs, SSO), and a cost/latency sketch for your 200 in / 150 out typical prompt. Priya will run an initial latency/cost estimate for a 512 token scenario on a dedicated pool.

[00:08:39] Maya Flores: Sounds good. Can we get the pilot kickoff scheduled for the week of May 11th? That's when we have bandwidth.

[00:08:46] Jordan Kim: Yep, I'll send a Doodle and propose May 11th as the kickoff.

[00:08:52] Elliot Wu: I'll prepare and share our traffic spreadsheet and a redaction plan for PII.

[00:08:58] Liam O'Connor: And Jordan, please include examples of latency numbers from customers in retail verticals if possible.

[00:09:05] Jordan Kim: Will do. Anything else?

[00:09:09] Maya Flores: One last one—do you support private model variants, like a quantized customer-owned model?

[00:09:17] Priya Desai: Yes, for private/dedicated we can onboard custom model artifacts and help with quantization recommendations. For hosted, we offer curated open models only.

[00:09:26] Jordan Kim: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up by end of day tomorrow with the packet and links.

[00:09:33] Maya Flores: Thanks Jordan, thanks Priya. Looking forward.

[00:09:36] Jordan Kim: Thanks, bye.

[00:09:40] (recording ends)
